name: Iraq

facts.religion: Shia Islam about 60%, Sunni about 35%, Christian and Yazidi minorities

system_note: Posts are informally shared among Shia, Sunni and Kurdish blocs.
snapshot: Iraq became a battlefield again as Iran-aligned militias traded fire with US forces, and it took until April to elect a president and pick a prime minister after the 2025 election.
culture: Iraq is ancient Mesopotamia, where writing, cities and law codes began, and Baghdad was the cultural capital of the Islamic world under the Abbasids. Najaf and Karbala are the holiest Shia cities, drawing millions of pilgrims for Arbaeen. Iraqi maqam music and poetry, and a love of football, unite a divided country. The Kurdistan Region has its own language, parliament and flag.
society: Oil provides almost all government revenue and pays millions of public salaries. Decades of war, sanctions, the 2003 US invasion and the fight against ISIS have left infrastructure battered. Summer power cuts and water shortages, worsened by dams upstream in Turkey and Iran, spark protests. Iran-aligned militias are formally part of the state through the Popular Mobilisation Forces.
situation: Iraq has spent two decades since the 2003 US invasion trying to be friends with both Washington and Tehran, its two most powerful patrons and now enemies at war. In 2026 that balancing act came close to breaking.

After elections in November 2025, government formation stalled for months, partly because the dominant bloc of Shia parties nominated Nouri al-Maliki, a two-time former prime minister close to Iran, and Trump warned in January that the US would stop helping Iraq if Maliki returned (AFP via BSS). Then the Iran war began, and Iraq became a battlefield again: Iran-aligned militias fired on US bases and the US embassy, and on Jordan, while American strikes hit them back. On 11 April, parliament finally elected Nizar Amedi, a 58-year-old Kurdish former environment minister, as president with 227 votes. "This ongoing conflict is not Iraq's war," he said, urging parties to keep the country out of it (Peregraf). Later that month, the US put bounties on two militia leaders, and the Shia bloc named businessman Ali al-Zaidi as prime minister-designate instead of Maliki (ISHM). Behind the politics, Iraq faces a slower crisis Amedi knows well from his last job: its rivers are drying up as upstream dams and climate change cut the flow of the Tigris and Euphrates.
power: A federal parliamentary republic with an informal sectarian power-sharing rule: the prime minister, who holds real power, is a Shia Arab; the speaker a Sunni Arab; and the largely ceremonial president a Kurd. The 329-seat Council of Representatives elects the president, who then nominates a prime minister. The Kurdistan Region has its own government.
holders: President Nizar Amedi (PUK), since April 2026; Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, whose government parliament approved in May 2026 and completed in October.

sources.label: Al Jazeera: parliament approves al-Zaidi government
